blocks.text: Pure water boiling in a kettle can be condensed straight back to water. But once a piece of yam is fried, no amount of cooling will give you raw yam again. Chemistry draws a hard line between these two kinds of change, and knowing which side a change falls on earns easy marks.

blocks.markdown:
## Two kinds of change

A **physical change** alters only the form or appearance of a substance. No new substance is formed, the change is usually easy to reverse, and the mass and chemical identity stay the same.

A **chemical change** produces one or more new substances with new properties. It is usually difficult to reverse and is normally accompanied by an energy change.

rows: Usually large; heat given out or taken in
Unchanged overall, but redistributed among new substances
Melting ice, dissolving salt, magnetising iron
Burning magnesium, rusting iron, souring of milk
blocks.caption: Distinguishing physical from chemical change

blocks.title: Dissolving is physical, not chemical
blocks.text: When common salt dissolves in water no new substance is made — evaporating the water returns the salt unchanged. Students often call dissolving a chemical change because the salt 'disappears'. It has not; it has only dispersed as ions among the water molecules.

blocks.markdown:
## Classifying matter

All matter is either a **pure substance** or a **mixture**.

- An **element** cannot be split into anything simpler by chemical means. It contains only one kind of atom. Examples: iron, oxygen, sulphur.
- A **compound** contains two or more elements chemically combined in a **fixed** ratio by mass. Examples: water (H2O), sodium chloride (NaCl), carbon dioxide (CO2).
- A **mixture** contains two or more substances physically together in any proportion. Examples: air, sea water, brass, crude oil.

blocks.caption: The classic iron and sulphur comparison

blocks.title: Iron and sulphur: mixture or compound?
blocks.prompt: Iron filings are stirred with sulphur powder. The mixture is then heated strongly until it glows red and continues glowing after the flame is removed. Explain what has happened at each stage.

steps.text: Before heating, the grey iron and yellow sulphur are simply intermingled. A magnet still pulls the iron out and carbon disulphide still dissolves the sulphur, so both keep their own properties. This is a mixture.
The proportions can be anything the student chooses, which confirms it is a mixture rather than a compound.
On strong heating the iron and sulphur react. The reaction is exothermic, which is why the glow continues once started: Fe + S -> FeS.
The black solid produced is iron(II) sulphide. A magnet no longer separates the iron and carbon disulphide no longer extracts the sulphur, so the properties are new.
The elements have combined in the fixed mass ratio 56 : 32, that is 7 : 4, which is a hallmark of a compound.

blocks.answer: Heating converts a mixture of iron and sulphur into the compound iron(II) sulphide, FeS, which has new properties and a fixed 7 : 4 mass ratio.

items: Evolution of a gas that was not there before, such as effervescence
A permanent colour change, not just a shade change
Formation of a precipitate when two clear solutions are mixed
A noticeable release or absorption of heat or light
The change cannot be reversed by simple physical means

blocks.title: Borderline cases WAEC loves
blocks.text: Melting candle wax is physical, but burning it is chemical. Dissolving sugar is physical, but caramelising it is chemical. Dissolving carbon dioxide in water is borderline because carbonic acid forms, so examiners describe it as chemical. Read the verb carefully before deciding.

points: A physical change makes no new substance and is easily reversed.
A chemical change makes at least one new substance and involves a definite energy change.
Elements contain one kind of atom; compounds contain elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
A mixture has variable composition, keeps the properties of its components and is separated physically.
Gas evolution, precipitate formation, permanent colour change and heat release are signs of a chemical change.
